search_path: /MPM SPH buoyancy force overestimation and hydrostatic validation benchmarks
exported_by: slot d14-corpusbib; inspect_deep_searches + get_paper_info, Undermind MCP, workspace read live
goal: Validating an MPM fluid solver against static buoyancy. A rigid sphere of radius 0.15 m held FIXED at its design waterline, exactly half submerged, in weakly compressible water. Vertical reaction measured from momentum exchange with an SDF collider: accumulated impulse needed to project fluid velocities out of the solid region, divided by the timestep. Measured force is about 50 percent LARGER than analytic rho*g*V_sub. Two explanations ruled out: particle leakage (reduced from 4.5 percent to 0.008 percent of particles, 49 of 598505, and the overestimate is still about 36 percent, so removing 99.8 percent of the leak removed only 30 percent of the error) and domain confinement (quadrupling tank plan area moved the ratio by 1 percent). EOS is weakly compressible p = -K*(J^-gamma - 1) with sound speed about 13 m/s rather than 1500 m/s. Quadratic B-spline basis, sphere spans about 16 cells across its diameter, g = 9.81. Asks what systematically causes a large positive bias in measured steady vertical force on a fixed body in MPM and SPH, and how published papers actually validate hydrostatic buoyancy and floating-body equilibrium: which canonical benchmarks, what error they treat as acceptable, how they measure the force, over what averaging window, and what convergence study.
summary: The strongest literature signal is that a large positive buoyancy bias is more plausibly a discrete hydrostatic/interface-coupling error than a tank-size effect, but the supplied studies DO NOT establish a universal 50 percent bias and DO NOT show that velocity-projection impulse exchange intrinsically double-counts gravity [Yan17, Yan18, Ste00, Bau23]. In MPM, hydrostatic validation is explicitly used to expose integration, pressure-oscillation, volumetric-locking and cell-crossing errors; quadratic B-splines and generalized interpolation reduce these but do not eliminate particle-location and quadrature sensitivity [Ste00, Ste08, Wal07, Che18c]. Reduced-sound-speed WCMPM is a credible contributor through compressibility and pressure transients, and incompressible/projection MPM was introduced specifically because WCMPM performs poorly at free surfaces; the retrieved papers give NO quantitative mapping from sound speed to steady buoyancy bias [Zha17c]. Free-surface pressure treatment is similarly central [Zha17c, Ski13]. SPH work confirms boundary treatment, pressure formulation, resolution and domain geometry materially affect body loads [Gar19, Jou20, Gun14]. The most reproducible published floating-body benchmark is Kramer et al.'s 300-mm sphere ballasted to half submergence, three heave-decay amplitudes, public time series, experimental uncertainty about 0.3 percent of drop height, BUT THIS IS A MOTION BENCHMARK, NOT A STATED STATIC-FORCE TOLERANCE [Kra21b, Sci19]. For static verification, MPM hydrostatic columns and SPH still-water pressure or fixed/floating-cylinder tests are more direct [Yan17, Gar19, Omi17, Qui18b]. The retrieved literature RARELY reports force-extraction windows, pressure-surface versus impulse-exchange cross-checks, or systematic particles-per-cell convergence, leaving those as essential diagnostics.
